title: Early Flu Season and Mutated H1N1 Strain Raise Concern for Younger Americans
excerpt: CDC data show flu positivity at 5.0% nationally and 10.7% on the West Coast, with H1N1 accounting for 96.4% of subtyped flu A viruses. Doctors recommend vaccination for everyone 6 months and older before the end of October.
body:
• Get a flu shot now, ideally before the end of October: the CDC and the American Medical Association recommend vaccination for everyone aged 6 months and older, and protection takes about two weeks to build.
  • Adults 65 and older should ask for Fluzone High-Dose, Flublok or Fluad if available; children 6 months through 8 years vaccinated for the first time may need two doses four weeks apart.
  • The dominant strain so far is influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 — 96.4% of subtyped flu A viruses in CDC data for the week ending October 10 — and a new G155E mutation may leave younger people with less residual protection.
  • Flu test positivity reached 5.0% nationally in the week ending October 10, up from 3.9% the week before, and 10.7% on the West Coast, compared with 0.5% a year earlier on the West Coast.

Doctors are urging Americans aged 6 months and older to get vaccinated against influenza after an early rise in cases on the West Coast and laboratory data showing a mutated H1N1 strain as the dominant virus so far this season.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its FluView report for the week ending October 10 that flu activity remains low nationally but has been increasing since late August, with the highest activity on the West Coast. Activity is higher than typically observed at this time of year but within expected seasonal variation, the agency said.

Clinical laboratories reported 2,270 positive specimens in the week ending October 10, or 5.0% of specimens tested, up from 3.9% the week before — a 10-year high for this time of year, Reuters reported. West Coast positivity was 10.7%, compared with 0.5% a year earlier; at a season's peak, positivity is around 30%.

Of flu A viruses subtyped in the week ending October 10, 242 of 251, or 96.4%, were A(H1N1)pdm09, the strain that caused the 2009 pandemic and is now a standard vaccine component. Last season was dominated by H3N2.

"What people are a bit worried about is that the H1N1 strain this year hasn't been seen by a lot of younger folk, so it may be more severe in them."

— Dr. Jennifer Duchon, Pediatric Infectious Disease Expert, Mount Sinai Children's Hospital

Researchers point to two possible explanations. This year's H1N1 virus carries a new mutation called G155E, and people exposed to earlier H1N1 versions may have only some residual protection, scientists told Reuters. Jeanne Marrazzo, chief executive of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, said small studies found antibodies from people exposed to flu last year did not recognize the new mutation, especially in teens and young adults — a reason for awareness, not alarm. Caitlin Rivers, a Johns Hopkins epidemiologist, cited an immunological gap after last year's H3N2 dominance and noted the unusual geography: cases typically start in the South and move north, while this year activity is coming from the west.

Last season, an estimated 32 million Americans had flu, 390,000 were hospitalized and 24,000 died, Reuters reported. Vaccine effectiveness against hospitalizations and deaths has ranged between 30% and 60% over the past 10 years. Scott Hensley, a microbiologist at the University of Pennsylvania, told Reuters two of the three components of this year's vaccine appear very well matched to circulating strains, but the H1N1 mutation might affect antibodies in younger people, making early vaccination a good idea.

The 2026-2027 vaccines, approved by the Food and Drug Administration in August, target H1N1, H3N2 and one influenza B virus. The CDC's vaccine guidance recommends vaccination for everyone 6 months and older with rare exceptions, ideally in September or October, and preferentially recommends Fluzone High-Dose, Flublok and Fluad for people 65 and older. Prescription antivirals work best when started as early as possible, especially for higher-risk patients, the CDC notes.

Uptake is the weak point. About 58 million adults received a flu shot last season, according to IQVIA data cited by Reuters, down more than 20% from nearly 75 million in 2019-20. Around half of U.S. children were vaccinated last year, compared with more than 60% in 2019-20. Reuters reported that flu-shot promotion has been reduced under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and that the CDC pulled its flu vaccination advertising campaign in 2025. An HHS spokesperson pointed Reuters to the CDC's Respiratory Illness Season Toolkit, which calls vaccination the most effective tool to prevent serious illness.

For Indian American households caring for young children and older parents together, timing matters. Vaccination before the end of October gives protection time to build, and babies under 6 months, who cannot be vaccinated, depend on vaccinated family and caregivers. Higher-risk patients should contact a clinician early about antivirals if symptoms develop.
